lines.text: One letter. Read once, in a fraction of a second.
But a bank doesn't get one letter.
It gets thousands every hour. A million every day.
And every single one of them needs a decision.
So here's the puzzle. Out of a million letters, how many should a person read?
The safe answer: all of them.
At a few minutes a letter, that's thousands of people, reading all day, every day.
The fast answer: none of them. Let the machine decide everything.
But remember the promise. At ninety-one percent, nine letters in a hundred are wrong.
Nine in a hundred, out of a million, is ninety thousand mistakes. Every single day.
Neither answer is right, because neither one counts the cost.
A person reading a letter costs something. Let's say, two euros.
A mistake costs more. A fraud report filed under billing. A frozen card. An angry customer. Say, twenty euros.
Now take one letter that Jev is p sure about.
If Jev decides, it's wrong with a chance of one minus p. And a mistake costs twenty.
If a person reads it, it costs two. Every time.
So a person should read it only when the risk costs more than the review.
One minus p, times twenty, is more than two. So p is below zero point nine.
Ninety percent. That line isn't a feeling. It falls out of two prices.
Change the prices, and the line moves.
Sorting newsletters? Mistakes are cheap. The line drops, and the machine takes almost everything.
Freezing someone's card? Mistakes are expensive. The line climbs, and almost everything goes to a person.
Back to our million letters. Here's how sure Jev is about each one.
Everything above the line, Jev handles. Everything below it goes to a person.
That's about a hundred and seventy thousand letters. Not a million. Not zero.
All of this only works if ninety percent really means ninety percent.
If Jev says ninety, but it's right only eighty times in a hundred, the math sends letters to the wrong place.
So the machine reads the million.
And people read the letters where they matter.
